destinations.timing_truths: En Route Truth: Spring (cherry blossoms) and autumn (koyo) are visually stunning but exponentially more crowded. Winter (January-February) is Tokyo's best-kept secret: crisp, clear skies (giving you the best views of Mt. Fuji), zero humidity, and immediate access to the city's legendary dining scene. | September is peak typhoon season; expect travel disruptions.
destinations.common_pitfalls: Believing your hotel concierge can get you into any restaurant at the last minute. The top-tier sushi and kaiseki spots require booking via specific platforms exactly 30 or 60 days out at midnight Japan time. | Carrying only credit cards; while improving, many small ramen shops and bars remain cash-only.
destinations.signature_moments: Walking through the hyper-modern Azabudai Hills at night, transitioning seamlessly from futuristic architecture to a centuries-old, serene Kaiseki dining room. | Standing in the exact center of the Shibuya Crossing at rush hour.
destinations.unique_insights: Tokyo is not one city; it is 15 distinct cities connected by trains. Group your days geographically (e.g., Shibuya/Harajuku on Day 1, Ginza/Tsukiji on Day 2) to avoid spending half your trip underground. | Taxis are immaculate and drivers wear white gloves, but they are very expensive; the subway is the true luxury hack for speed.
highlights_arr: Pre-dawn visit to the Toyosu fish market followed by a masterclass sushi breakfast
Shibuya Sky timed entry near sunset for a full-city neon glow
Discovering an eight-seat, unmarked whiskey bar in Ginza
Staying at hyper-luxury urban sanctuaries like Aman Tokyo or Janu
Immersive digital art experiences at teamLab Borderless in Azabudai Hills
Curated shopping through the flagship designer boutiques of Omotesando

destinations.timing_truths: En Route Truth: Cherry blossom forecasts shift every year, and peak bloom brings absolute chaos. The real secret is late November: the autumn foliage (koyo) is stunning, the air is crisp, and the spring crowd chaos is absent. | Summer in the Kyoto basin is a brutally humid, stagnant oven; avoid July and August entirely.
destinations.common_pitfalls: Temple fatigue. Planning to visit five temples a day will leave you exhausted and numb to their beauty. Relying on public transport during Golden Week (late April) guarantees gridlock. | Harassing geisha in the Gion district for photos; it is highly disrespectful and now strictly policed with fines.
destinations.signature_moments: Walking the Philosopher's Path before the tour buses arrive, feeling the profound, meditative silence that defined the ancient capital. | Watching a Maiko perform a traditional dance in a private tatami room during a multi-course Kaiseki dinner.
destinations.unique_insights: True luxury in Kyoto isn't just about budget; it's about access. The absolute best ryokans, like Tawaraya, do not operate on standard hotel booking engines. They open their books exactly six months out and sell out within hours. | The city grid is massive; you must group your temple visits geographically.
highlights_arr: Arashiyama bamboo forest at 6:30 AM, followed by a quiet garden detour
Fushimi Inari at dusk/night for a lantern-lit, crowd-free atmosphere
Private tea ceremony with an etiquette primer in a historic machiya
Staying at world-class luxury properties like Aman Kyoto or Tawaraya
Exclusive geisha (geiko) dinner arranged through top-tier concierges
Walking the Philosopher's Path during the peak autumn koyo season

destinations.timing_truths: En Route Truth: Summer (June-August) brings brutal, suffocating humidity and monsoon rains. You must visit in the crisp, stunning windows of Spring (Cherry Blossoms) or Autumn (Fall Foliage).
destinations.common_pitfalls: Treating Osaka just like Tokyo. The culture here is Kuidaore (eat until you drop). Do not over-schedule museums and shrines here; your entire itinerary should be aggressively focused on food and nightlife.
destinations.signature_moments: Standing beneath the massive, glowing neon signs of Dotonbori, eating street food that rivals Michelin-starred restaurants, realizing Osaka is the true beating heart of Japanese culture.
destinations.unique_insights: If Tokyo is Japan's brain, Osaka is its stomach. It is louder, friendlier, and less formal than Tokyo. Because Kyoto has become overwhelmingly crowded, ultra-luxe travelers are now anchoring in Osaka's superior 5-star hotels and day-tripping to Kyoto.
highlights_arr: Using the city as a frictionless, high-speed rail base for the Suzuka F1 Grand Prix
Diving into the neon-drenched, culinary chaos of Dotonbori at midnight
Eating impossibly elevated Takoyaki and Okonomiyaki in hidden, 4-seat restaurants
Staying in the sleek, sky-high luxury of the Conrad or St. Regis Osaka
Taking a quick 45-minute bullet train for a day trip to the ancient temples of Kyoto
